title: Concept-Agnostic Attention Module Discovery
one_liner: Find which parts of a transformer handle a given concept by measuring how each attention head matches the concept's pattern, then control those parts with a single number.
lead: Transformers are black boxes — you give them text or an image and get an answer, but you cannot see how they think. This paper opens a window by finding exactly which attention heads (the parts that let the model focus on relevant pieces of its input) handle specific concepts like safety or reasoning. Once you find those heads, you can dial them up or down with one number to amplify or suppress that concept.

problem.h2: The attention heads are a mystery
paras: Transformers rely on attention heads — parts of the model that learn to focus on relevant pieces of the input. But today we cannot point to a specific head and say what it does. We can see that removing an entire layer hurts performance, but not which individual heads matter for which concepts.

A beginner might think: remove each head one at a time, measure what breaks, and infer what each head does. That works, but it is slow — a transformer with many layers and heads requires thousands of experiments. We need a fast way to find the heads without trial and error.

callout.html: Represent a concept (like safety or reasoning) as a pattern, measure which attention heads match that pattern best, group those heads as a module, and adjust them all with one dial.

panels.title: 1. A concept is a pattern
panels.caption: Safety is a pattern: words about harm, refusal, ethical rules.

panels.title: 2. Each head outputs a pattern too
panels.caption: Each attention head processes input words and emits a pattern. Does it match safety?

panels.title: 3. Measure similarity: high = good match
panels.caption: Compare each head's pattern to the safety pattern using similarity scoring.

panels.title: 4. Select the best heads
panels.caption: Pick the top-scoring heads — they form the safety module.

panels.title: 5. Dial the module up or down
panels.viz_args: Dial = 0.5x: weaker safety | Dial = 2.0x: stronger safety
panels.caption: Adjust all selected heads together with one number to control behavior.

steps.text: Average the model's internal activations on examples that show the concept (e.g., safe responses) to get one pattern (a list of numbers).
For each attention head in each layer, measure how similar its output is to the concept pattern by checking if they point in the same direction.
Select the K heads with the highest similarity scores across all layers — they form the concept module.
Multiply the outputs of just those heads by a dial number: use 0.5 to weaken them, 1.0 for normal, or 2.0 to strengthen them. The model recomputes with the adjusted heads.
See how dialing the concept up or down changes the model's behavior on downstream tasks.

paras: The paper changes which attention heads get adjusted during intervention. Instead of retraining the whole model or steering the entire hidden state, it isolates a small set of heads that handle one concept and dials those up or down.

hidden.name: Directional match score between concept and head
paras: A concept (like safety) leaves a fingerprint in the model's activations — a specific pattern. Each attention head also produces a pattern. The method measures how much the head's pattern matches the concept's pattern by checking if they point in the same direction.

The paper estimates this similarity by running the model on a dataset of examples that showcase the concept, collecting the output from each attention head, and computing the mathematical similarity between that output and the averaged concept pattern.

heat.caption: Darker means higher similarity to the concept. Highlighted heads (layer 2, layer 4, layer 5) form the module.

reads.html: The paper finds which parts of the model handle a concept by looking for heads whose outputs match the concept's pattern.
Directional match score (how aligned two lists of numbers are) between the concept pattern and each attention head's contribution, computed by averaging across a dataset.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the causal chain
paras: Attention heads specialize during training. A head learns to focus on certain word pairs or patterns because they help the model make better predictions. Over time, heads that contribute to the same concept converge on similar patterns. So if you measure which heads are similar to a concept, you are finding the heads that learned to handle that concept.

When you adjust those heads with a dial number (multiply by 0.5 to weaken, 2.0 to strengthen), you are changing their influence on the internal state that flows to the next layer. Amplifying the safety heads makes the model more cautious; suppressing them makes it easier to jailbreak. The reason this works is that each head's contribution is additive — turning down the safety heads removes their voice without breaking the computational flow of the rest of the model.

stages.s: Text or image (split into pieces for processing)
Compare each head to concept pattern
Adjust selected heads by dial number
Output with concept dialed up or down

math.words: For each attention head in each layer, compute the cosine similarity between the head's output and the vectorized concept. Select the K heads with the highest similarity. For intervention, multiply the selected heads' contributions by a scalar factor.
math.equation:
similarity(h) = (concept . head_h) / (||concept|| * ||head_h||)

module = TopK heads by similarity(h)

adjusted_output = sum over selected heads (s * head_contribution) + sum over other heads (head_contribution)
symbols: the averaged pattern of the concept, as a list of numbers
the output of attention head h, as a list of numbers
dot product: multiply corresponding numbers and add them up
length of the list (how far it stretches in space)
how much two lists point in the same direction, from 0 to 1
the scalar dial: 1.0 = normal, 0.5 = weaker, 2.0 = stronger
the K heads with the highest similarity scores

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: similarity(head_3) = 1.08 / (1.0 * 1.0) = 1.08 (clamped to 1.0 in practice: very high match)
With dial s=0.5, head 3 contributes only half as much to the next layer.

math.note: The directional match captures how aligned two patterns are; higher means the head is more central to that concept. The dial number scales that head's strength proportionally.

charts.title: Without intervention (baseline)
charts.note: Model is neither very safe nor very good at reasoning — default behavior.

charts.title: With SAMI: amplify reasoning
charts.note: Dial reasoning up by 1.6x: the reasoning heads contribute more, making the model solve more math problems (+1.6% observed). Safety heads stay the same because we did not dial them.

charts.title: With SAMI: suppress safety
charts.note: Dial safety down to 0.5x: model becomes much easier to jailbreak (72.7% success rise).

items.html: If two concepts share heads, adjusting one affects the other. The paper does not fully address crosstalk between overlapping modules.
The concept pattern is built from a small reference dataset. If the dataset does not represent the concept well, the whole method fails silently.
The method finds heads at one layer that match the concept. It may miss important contributions from other layers if they process the concept differently.

Use a diverse, representative dataset for the concept. Pick K (the number of heads) large enough to capture the full module but small enough to avoid noise. Validate by checking that the intervention actually changes behavior as expected.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple transformer on a toy task (like sentiment classification). Pick a clear concept (e.g., positive vs negative words). Run SAMD to find the heads that match that concept pattern. Then use SAMI to dial those heads up and down and watch the model's predictions flip accordingly. Log which heads were selected and verify they stay consistent if you train the same model twice.
demo.metric_eq:
module_stability = fraction of selected heads that are the same across two independent runs

concept_effect = sentiment accuracy with dial=2.0 minus sentiment accuracy with dial=0.5
demo.closing: The core claim: the same small set of heads reliably handles one concept, and you can control them with a single number without retraining.
